frameworks.notes: Research (step 2): STAR = Situation, Task, Action, Result; the behavioural-interview decomposition popularised through DDI's Targeted Selection (1970s), used for interview answers, resume bullets (PAR / CAR variants: Problem or Context, Action, Result) and performance reviews; STARR / STARL add Reflection or Learning. Situation forces the starting conditions and stakes; Task forces the actor's own objective and responsibility and is the slot most often left implicit; Action forces concrete first-person steps; Result forces a measurable outcome attributed to the action. tbpn_example.episode_title: Apple Goes Full Throttle on F1, Meme Stocks Make a Comeback, Amazon's New Wearable AI Device (Christina Cacioppo, Deena Shakir, Davide Asnaghi, Ylan Richard)

frameworks.notes: Research: CARL = Context, Action, Result, Learning, a reflective-practice variant of STAR (health-professions and education reflection toolkits, competency interviews) that replaces Situation/Task with Context and adds a Learning slot. The registry adds a fifth slot, rule: the double-loop lesson after Argyris and Schon (Organizational Learning, 1978; Argyris, 'Double Loop Learning in Organizations', HBR 1977). Single loop corrects the action inside the governing variables (the thermostat turns the heat on); double loop questions the governing variable itself (why 68 degrees). Common misuse: Learning restated as the Result, or a single-loop 'be more careful' written as if it were a systemic rule. Classic example planned: a reflective-practice case from the domain CARL is taught in (a medication near-miss on a ward), where the single-loop learning is personal vigilance and the double-loop rule changes the storage policy. Decision: scout prompt is Part B verbatim plus the scratchpad line Part A requires and one sentence saying what a completed CARL event looks like in speech. Scout (step 3): three candidates returned: (1) Cala's shutdown post-mortem, 2025-07-23; (2) Perplexity's shopping/commerce misfire, Aravind Srinivas, 2025-04-23; (3) Mike Krieger on what Artifact taught him, 2025-09-29. Chose (1): a completed eight-year episode narrated by the founder two months after the shutdown, with the rare property CARL needs most, namely that every operating measure he gives succeeded (five very profitable restaurants, 60% retention, 95% satisfaction, the only proven payback on a robotic install) while the company still died, so the correction has to be made one loop up; he also names the governing assumption that failed ('we did not understand that when we created the business and structured the business') and then states four forward rules for the company he is incorporating, which gives the graph fact nodes in Learning and in Systemic rule and lets the derived nodes be the loop diagnosis and the market reading rather than the whole right-hand side. (2) was a close second and is the tightest chain in the corpus (stated governing assumption, shipped action, stated failure mode, explicit 'what we learned the hard way', explicit 'so that's my lesson from this'), but its double loop is a product-strategy correction rather than a change to a governing structure; kept as the fallback if a reviewer rejects (1). Correction to the scout: it attributed the Cala segment to Davide Asnaghi. L5844 introduces the guest as 'Elan' and the extraction's people list credits the Cala shutdown story to 'Elan (Ylan)', i.e. Ylan Richard, the last guest in the episode title; Davide Asnaghi is the Diodes/PCB guest in the same episode. All source_refs say Ylan Richard. Entity spelling: companies use the extraction spellings ('Cala', 'Sweetgreen'); the speaker is not listed in entities because the extraction spells him 'Elan (Ylan)', a transcription artefact rather than a name a future merge should key on. Idea-bearing slot: rule, the double-loop slot, where both derived nodes carry an idea (u5 formation-stack tooling that prices wind-down liability at incorporation, u6 the European Series A/B cliff as an underserved capital market). Graph (step 4): validate.mjs PASS, 0 errors, 0 warnings on the first run. classic 16 nodes (12 fact / 4 derived), 20 edges (3 fact / 17 derived); tbpn 27 nodes (21 fact / 6 derived), 34 edges (7 fact / 27 derived). Provenance rule applied to edges: fact only where one contiguous span states the connection ('but in the end, managed to have', 'And so the thinking from there was', 'got hung on', 'prevented us from doing that', 'And so ultimately', 'and we should have understood'); every generalizes_to edge from Learning to Systemic rule is derived, because the double-loop generalisation is precisely the inference the framework exists to make explicit. Design decision: the classic example is a nursing reflective-practice near miss, the genre CARL is actually taught in, and it mirrors the TBPN case structurally (a single-loop resolution about personal care superseded by a change to where the drugs are stored). Relations: kept the registry's four (motivates, produces, teaches, generalizes_to) and added constrains, needed for the two cases where a stated context condition blocks an action (French regulation preventing the restructure, the funding cliff hitting the scaling decision). frameworks.name: Minto SCQA

tbpn_example.episode_title: xAI merges with X, Isomorphic Labs raises $600M (Aaron Levie, Alexis Ohanian, RJ Halperin, Cristobal Valenzuela, David Zagaynov, Sam Lessin)

frameworks.notes: Start (step 1): read SPEC.md, AGENT_BRIEF.md, the minto-scqa registry entry (slots situation/complication/question/answer; relations disrupted_by/raises/answered_by; layout hint tree, direction right, chain S -> C -> Q -> A) and schema.json; read toulmin-model and star-par (both done) for house style, with SPEC.md winning where they predate the current conventions (fact edges, idea field, source_ref line ranges, Example 2 section split). Research (step 2, recall): Barbara Minto, McKinsey, The Pyramid Principle (1970s course; book 1987, revised 1996): the introduction told as a story so that the reader arrives at the writer's main point with the question already in mind. Situation = a self-contained, non-controversial statement about the subject that the reader already knows and accepts (time, place, stable baseline: 'you know that...'). Complication = what happened in that situation to disturb it and create a need: something went wrong, something changed, something new arrived, someone proposed an alternative, results fell short. Question = the single question the complication raises in the reader's mind (what should we do; how do we do it; is the proposal right; why did it not work); usually implicit, never more than one. Answer = the main point, the governing thought at the top of the pyramid; stated in a written memo, and it raises a new question (why? how?) answered by the key line, which is where the Pyramid Principle proper takes over. Minto's pattern table: need to do task / something prevents / what to do; have problem / know solution / how to implement; have problem / solution proposed / is it right; took action / did not work / why not; took action / worked / how to get more. Orders: standard S-C-A, direct A-S-C, concerned C-S-A, aggressive Q-S-C-A. Common misuse: situation that smuggles in the complication or the answer; a complication that is a list of problems with no single question; a question the answer does not answer; an answer that is a topic ('our pricing') rather than a point; assuming the reader accepts a contested situation; the question left so vague that any answer fits. Provenance expectation: situation and complication are usually stated (speakers narrate how it was and what changed); the question is almost never stated (derived, high confidence when the complication is sharp); the answer is stated when the speaker is pitching (fact) but the answer at the level of the question, or the resolution of a discussion nobody closed, is derived. Idea-bearing slot candidate: answer (the resolution a complication forces is the pitch), to be confirmed after the scout. Scout (step 3): three candidates returned, all outside the two episodes already used by siblings (2025-11-19 Hutchins for toulmin-model, 2025-07-14 Windsurf for star-par): (1) Poseidon / David Zagaynov, the ekranoplan 'flying boats' pitch, 2025-03-31; (2) Arena AI / Pratap Ranade, Atlas AI hardware engineer, 2025-04-08; (3) Orchid Health / Noor Siddiqui, whole-genome embryo screening, 2025-08-18. Chose (1) Poseidon: the founder narrates the whole SCQA in sequence in one contiguous passage (L5614-L5698) - a hundred-year-stable logistics baseline, two distinct complications (the Soviet ekranoplan blockers dissolved by composites and modern controls; ground-effect craft fall under the Coast Guard and IMO rather than the FAA), and a one-sentence governing thought ('So what we're building are flying boats') with hard numbers later (50 ft, two tons, a quarter to a third of air-freight price per kg-mile). Decisive for this library: TWO questions are spoken aloud in the passage and NEITHER is the Minto question - the founder voices a premature search question raised by the situation alone (L5630) and a host voices a 'why now' question about the complication (L5802-L5808) - so the graph can show fact question nodes beside the derived one and make the framework's signature provenance point visible. (2) was a close second (canonical unstated question, sharpest numbers) and is the fallback if a reviewer rejects (1). Decision: idea_bearing_slot = question, not answer as the research step guessed: in a TBPN founder pitch the answer is almost always stated (a fact node, and facts may not carry an idea), while the question the complication forces is the slot that names the underserved need and generalises into a market screen. Graph (step 4): validate.mjs PASS, 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 paraphrases; every quote extracted from the transcript by line range with a script that asserts the normalised span is present in the source, so no quote was typed by hand. classic = 10 nodes (7 fact / 3 derived), 14 edges (4 fact / 10 derived): an original Minto-pattern memo scenario (Fielding Instruments) written so that the Question is genuinely absent from the source text - the narration says only that she never puts the question on the page - which keeps the framework's signature slot derived. tbpn = 21 nodes (16 fact / 5 derived), 33 edges (4 fact / 29 derived). Design decisions: (a) added a fourth relation, elaborates, to the registry's three, because SCQA slots hold several statements each and the intra-slot structure (c3 explains why c2 matters, a2 and a3 are the same answer at different scales) has nowhere else to go; the registry's slot ids and its three relations are unchanged. (b) The question slot carries two fact nodes (q0, the founder's premature search question raised by the situation alone, and q1, the host's spoken why-now question) beside two derived ones (q2, the Minto question; q3, the generalised market screen). Both spoken questions are answered by something other than the Answer - q1 by two complication facts (e19, e20) - which is the clearest way to show why the Minto question has to be derived even in a transcript full of question marks. (c) Fact edges are only the four where one speaker states the connection in a single contiguous span; every cross-speaker link and every narrative-order link is derived per SPEC 3, which is why the derived-edge count is high. (d) idea fields sit on q2 (0.85, the coastal-freight lane) and q3 (0.6, the cheaper-certifier screen), both in the idea-bearing slot. Viz loop (step 6): iteration 1 revise (blocking: a page-local #labels z-index garbled the panel and the tooltip), iteration 2 revise (blocking: the extension block re-did the engine-owned #labels stacking and double-rendered the idea marks with a page-local gold OPPORTUNITY tag), iteration 3 PASS 5/5/4/5 with no blocking issues. Everything else already matched: every node has a README entry with the right provenance tag and confidence, node texts, quotes and rationales are reproduced exactly, every non-supported_by edge id is cited, both idea sentences are quoted verbatim, and the classic source text is verbatim from graph.json. frameworks.name: Pyramid Principle

tbpn_example.episode_title: Sam Altman live on Sora, Hollywood, the future of ads (Bill Peebles, Dylan Patel, Elad Gil, Robby Stein, Morgan Housel, Misha Laskin)

frameworks.notes: Research (recall): Barbara Minto, McKinsey's first female MBA hire (1963), developed the method to teach consultants to write; The Pyramid Principle (in-house 1978, Pitman 1987; later The Minto Pyramid Principle: Logic in Writing, Thinking and Problem Solving, 1996/2009). Object: a piece of reasoning meant for a reader, arranged answer-first. Slots: governing thought (the single sentence that answers the reader's question and sits at the apex), key lines (the pillars; each answers the question the governing thought raises in the reader's mind: Why? How? How do you know?; together the set must be MECE, mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive, a term Minto coined; a set is either a deductive chain, premise, premise, therefore, or an inductive group of the same kind of idea under one plural noun such as reasons, steps, problems, ordered by time, structure or degree), supports (the data, quotes and observations under each pillar; the base of the pyramid). Three rules: ideas at any level summarise the ideas grouped below them; ideas in a grouping are the same kind of idea; ideas in a grouping are in logical order. Vertical logic is a question-and-answer dialogue with the reader; horizontal logic is deductive or inductive. Justification: Miller's seven-plus-or-minus-two; the reader's mind groups whatever it receives, so the writer should impose the grouping first. The introduction uses SCQ (Situation, Complication, Question), filed in this library under minto-scqa; the pyramid proper starts at the Answer. Textbook use: Minto's opening illustration, a secretary's phone message about rescheduling a meeting told in the order the calls came in, against its pyramid form (reschedule, because it suits the attendees and the room is free); and the consultant's recommendation memo with three pillars. Common misuse: bottom-up narration (the story of the analysis before the answer); topic headings instead of assertions ('Costs' rather than 'Costs are rising'); intellectually blank summaries ('there are three problems') that group without synthesising; overlapping or incomplete key lines (not MECE); mixing deductive and inductive in one group; more than about five key lines; a governing thought that does not answer the question the reader has. Provenance expectation: supports are stated (fact); key lines are stated when the speaker enumerates ('three reasons') and derived when the speaker narrates bottom-up and the summary must be written; the governing thought is usually derived because speakers rarely state their one-sentence answer first, and when a speaker does state it, the stated sentence is a fact node and the synthesis the pyramid requires is a derived node above it. Scout: three candidates returned: (1) Elad Gil's three-pillar case on why the AI market is mis-sized, 2025-10-10, L3116-L3210; (2) Sean Henry (Stord) 'our three pillars are really a network, software and scale', 2025-05-16; (3) a host reading the WSJ 'why there will never be another Warren Buffett' piece (the person, the period, the package), 2025-05-05. Chose (1). Reason: it is the interesting provenance case rather than the tidiest pyramid. The speaker enumerates his pillars ('the first thing... a second thing... the third thing'), so the key lines and their group membership are facts with quoted ordinal connectives, but he puts an intellectually blank label on top ('two or three things that are underappreciated') and reaches his conclusion only after the pillars, so the governing thought - the synthesis Minto requires - has to be written. (2) was the closest to a textbook answer-first pyramid but is a founder's pitch in which every level is stated, so almost nothing would be derived; (3) is a host reading someone else's argument aloud, which makes the speaker attribution fuzzy. Candidate (2) is recorded here as the better example if a later reviewer wants an all-fact pyramid. Research (recall): Stephen Toulmin, The Uses of Argument (1958), a model of practical, field-dependent argument as opposed to the syllogism. Six parts: Claim (what is to be accepted), Grounds/Data (the specific facts appealed to), Warrant (the general, bridge-like inference licence 'if D then C', normally left unstated), Backing (the field-specific assurance behind the warrant: statutes, statistics, expertise), Qualifier (modal strength: presumably, probably, necessarily), Rebuttal (conditions of exception under which the warrant does not license the step). Textbook case: Harry was born in Bermuda, so presumably Harry is a British subject, since a person born in Bermuda is generally a British subject, on account of the relevant statutes, unless both parents were aliens or he has been naturalised elsewhere. Native diagram: grounds at left, arrow to 'so, qualifier, claim' at right, warrant under the arrow ('since'), backing under the warrant ('on account of'), rebuttal hanging off the qualifier ('unless'). Common misuse: warrant restated as a specific claim rather than a general rule; backing confused with grounds (backing supports the warrant, not the claim); rebuttal confused with a counter-claim (it is a condition, not an opposing argument); qualifier dropped so every claim sounds certain. Provenance expectation: grounds and claim are usually stated (fact); warrant is almost always unstated (derived); backing is stated only when the speaker is pressed; qualifier is sometimes stated as a hedge ('probably', 'I think'); rebuttal is occasionally stated ('unless') but mostly derived. frameworks.notes: Research: MECE (Mutually Exclusive, Collectively Exhaustive) comes from Barbara Minto at McKinsey (1960s-70s), the grouping test inside the Pyramid Principle. It partitions a whole on ONE dimension so branches do not overlap (ME) and together cover the whole (CE). Classic uses: profit/cost trees, issue trees, market segmentation. Classic misuse: cutting on two dimensions at once (channel and geography) so items double-count; a catch-all 'Other' faking exhaustiveness; buckets that are MECE but carry no insight. Design decision: added one slot `cut` (typical_provenance derived) for the partitioning dimension, plus relation `cut_by` (whole -> cut). MECE's whole content is the choice of a single cutting dimension, and the registry itself says 'the partitioning principle is an LLM choice' inside the bucket description; giving it a node makes the choice inspectable and gives the tree its native four-level shape (whole / cut / buckets / items+gaps). frameworks.notes:
Research. Origin: the issue tree (logic tree, diagnostic tree) is the McKinsey problem-solving staple, formalised in Barbara Minto's Pyramid Principle (the same MECE grouping read top-down as a question rather than as an assertion), popularised in Ethan Rasiel's The McKinsey Way (1999) and given its modern textbook treatment in Conn and McLean, Bulletproof Problem Solving (2018). Two structures share one diagram. An ISSUE TREE decomposes a root question into mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive sub-questions and stops there; it is a map of what you would have to know. A HYPOTHESIS TREE goes one step further: each branch carries a candidate answer stated so that it could be wrong, plus the analysis that would show it wrong. Hypothesis-driven problem solving (the 'day one answer', the ghost pack) exists to stop the boil-the-ocean data gathering an issue tree alone invites: you do not collect everything, you collect the one observation that kills the most branches. What each slot forces: question forces a single decision-relevant question rather than a topic; issue forces siblings that are MECE, so that no cause hides between branches and no branch is counted twice; hypothesis forces a falsifiable sentence with a direction and a magnitude, not a subject heading; test forces the disconfirming observation, named in advance, with the threshold that would settle it; evidence forces the observation actually in hand, kept separate from the reading of it. Common misuse: hypotheses too vague to be wrong ('marketing is weak'); confirmation-seeking tests that look for supporting data instead of the killer; overlapping or incomplete siblings; the tree used as a work plan (tasks) rather than a logic structure (claims); deep trees that never reach an observation; and prioritising by ease of analysis rather than by which branch, if resolved, most moves the answer. Design consequence for provenance: the test slot is almost always derived, because sources volunteer explanations and almost never volunteer the observation that would kill their own explanation. That contrast is this framework's provenance story: with derived hidden the page shows a question and a heap of volunteered hypotheses with no tests under any of them (a wish list); with derived shown, the MECE issue scaffolding appears above them, the unstated sibling hypotheses appear beside them, and a test hangs under every hypothesis. Scout: launched with Part B plus a framework-specific addendum (what a live diagnostic question looks like, the demand for three or more volunteered candidate answers, quantitative observations that cut both ways, and an explicit warning off two-sided theses and single-chain root-cause narratives, which sibling frameworks own; also excluded the nine episode dates already claimed by sibling agents). It returned three ranked candidates. Chose #1, the 2025-08-09 weekly recap, because the hosts pose the diagnostic question in one sentence out loud, announce that several explanations exist, then volunteer five of them in one continuous segment, each with its own stated connective back to the question, and because the segment contains the rare thing this framework needs: one stated falsification condition. Rejected #2 (2025-09-08 Census AI adoption: excellent contradictory evidence but the root question is mangled in the transcript and the explanations are spread across two distant segments) and #3 (2025-12-10 venture fundraising: strong question, but the candidate answers are mostly speculative futures rather than explanations of the stated anomaly). Design decisions. (1) Kept all five registry slot ids and all four registry relations. Refined two slot descriptions: `hypothesis` typical_provenance is set to 'either' rather than 'derived', because the whole provenance story of this framework is that sources volunteer hypotheses freely (five fact hypotheses in the TBPN example, two in the classic) and never volunteer the test; and `bears_on` is described as running from an observation to a hypothesis or to the question the observation makes a puzzle, so the anomaly evidence can attach to the root. (2) The provenance contrast is deliberately built around the `test` slot: 12 of the 12 tests across both examples are derived except one (t_oai in the TBPN example, quoted verbatim), so hiding the derived layer leaves a question, the volunteered explanations connected by the speakers' own connectives, the evidence, and no way to tell any explanation from any other. That is the wish list the framework exists to replace. (3) The issue layer is entirely derived in both examples and is inserted between the question and the volunteered hypotheses, so the full view shows the MECE scaffolding the source never built. The four TBPN issues are MECE by construction on a ratio: the measurement misassigns work, the numerator genuinely rose, the denominator is capped by supply, the denominator is capped by demand. The demand branch is empty in the source, which is the sharpest single observation the tree produces. (4) idea_bearing_slot is `hypothesis`, with ideas on the two derived hypotheses h_blind (nobody can measure AI revenue) and h_pilot (enterprise AI stuck before production). (5) The classic case is a synthetic profitability diagnostic in the standard consulting form, written so the two volunteered explanations arrive without tests and the source states, in its last sentence, that nobody proposed a way to tell them apart. validate: 0 errors, 0 warnings on the first run. frameworks.name: First Principles Thinking

tbpn_example.episode_title: Dwarkesh Patel, Nadia Asparouhova, Augustus Doricko, Casey Handmer, Ishan Mukherjee, Mike Knoop; Trump pardons Milton, CoreWeave IPO winners

frameworks.notes:
Research (recall): first principle = Aristotle's arche, 'the first basis from which a thing is known', a proposition not deduced from any other; Descartes' method of doubt is the modern ancestor (reduce to what cannot be doubted, then rebuild). In engineering practice the method is: reason from physics, arithmetic and material or unit costs instead of from analogy and precedent. Five beats matching the registry slots: (1) problem, the question as posed, which usually arrives already carrying an inherited answer; (2) assumption, the borrowed belief being removed, normally sourced to industry precedent, an analogy or 'everyone knows'; (3) fundamental_truth, what survives deletion of the belief, a physical law, a spot material price, an arithmetic identity or a regulatory fact; (4) constraint, the bound those truths actually force, which is the step nobody shows their working for; (5) rebuilt_solution, what becomes buildable at that bound rather than at the precedent. Classic textbook use: the battery-pack argument. Common misuse: (a) 'first principles' as a badge for any bottom-up analysis that is still reasoning by analogy one level down; (b) stopping at a truth that is itself a convention (a market wage, a regulated tariff); (c) no assumption named, so nothing is stripped and there is no before-and-after; (d) reading the derived limit as a plan rather than a floor; (e) the cheaper-same-thing error, where an incremental cost reduction on the incumbent machine is relabelled a first-principles rebuild.

Provenance line for this framework (the point of the page): the precedent being stripped away is normally a fact, because someone says it out loud ('everyone knows X costs Y'), while the fundamental truths, the limits they imply and the rebuilt solution are normally derived. That inversion (the assumption is the datum; the reasoning that deletes it is the inference) is the interesting provenance story.

Scout / example decision: chose 2025-03-28, Casey Handmer (Terraform Industries, ex-NASA JPL) at L3228-L3458. He runs the method twice in one uninterrupted answer: nuclear's cost is stripped from the regulator to the turbine island ('even if NRC didn't exist tomorrow ... it would still be the case that just the steam engine component is going to cost no less than coal'), and space-based solar is killed not on launch cost, where that argument is normally had, but on a revenue-per-watt identity taken from Starlink. Both chains carry real numbers, so the derived-limit slot is fillable rather than decorative.

Deviation from the expected provenance line, deliberate and worth a reader's attention: because the speaker is a physicist reasoning out loud, six of the fundamental truths and four of the limits are stated, so they are facts, not inferences. The TBPN example therefore runs 17 fact / 8 derived. This is the honest reading of the source and it makes the page's contrast sharper rather than weaker: with derived hidden, what remains is a complete first-principles argument that a human actually performed, and the eight derived nodes are exactly the joints he skipped (a5 the fuel-versus-machine frame inside the question, t8 the pivot that a PV cell has no heat cycle, c5 the 200x-400x land ratio he never divides, c6 that licence reform cannot move a turbine-set floor, c7 the allocation argument joining the revenue ratio to his conclusion, r4/r5/r6 the buildable readings). frameworks.notes:
Research: Polya, How to Solve It (1945). Four phases - Understanding the problem (what is the unknown, what are the data, what is the condition), Devising a plan (find the connection, look for a related problem solved before, vary the problem), Carrying out the plan (check each step), Looking back (examine the solution, can the result or method be used for another problem). Phases are structural scaffolding with provenance schema and the engine's reserved grey. The registry's plan slot absorbs Polya's related problem: an analogy is a plan node with attrs.kind = analogy, linked by borrows_from. generalization is the idea-bearing slot because a heuristic that transfers is close to a product thesis. | Scout returned three candidates; chose rank 2 (2025-10-06) over rank 1 (2025-10-16 Botha VC arithmetic) for three reasons: the 2025-10-16 episode is already the TBPN source for wardley-mapping; the AMD passage is a single bounded sizing problem with a verbalised plan, which is the rarest Polya slot in speech; and its phase profile makes the page's point - two estimates are produced before any method exists, the method is then stated and never executed, and the Look back phase is empty of facts entirely. | validate: 0 errors, 0 warnings on the scaffold. | Added two relations to the registry's six, documented in the README: `states` (the problem as posed states the unknown, the data or the condition) and `uses` (a step or plan consumes a datum, a quantity from the problem, or the output of an earlier step). frameworks.name: Means-Ends Analysis

tbpn_example.episode_title: Astronomer CEO affair at Coldplay concert, Juul approved by the FDA, is AI causing historic crashouts (Chris Power, Jeremie Eliahou, Chris Best, Alex Mashrabov)

frameworks.notes:
Research: Means-Ends Analysis comes from Newell, Shaw and Simon's General Problem Solver (1959) and Simon & Newell's Human Problem Solving (1972). Core loop: compare current state to goal state, detect the most significant difference, select an operator known to reduce that difference, test the operator's preconditions; if a precondition is unmet, promote it to a sub-goal and recurse. Slots kept from the registry: current_state, goal_state, difference, operator, precondition, subgoal. The two states are usually stated; the difference that matters most, the precondition an operator needs, and the promotion of an unmet precondition to a sub-goal are the framework's own contribution and are derived. Recursion is the point: a sub-goal is a goal, so the structure nests. idea field lives on precondition and subgoal nodes (an unmet precondition nobody owns is often a business). Classic misuse: hill-climbing on the nearest difference and ignoring a large difference that needs a detour (the Tower of Hanoi / Missionaries-and-Cannibals trap where the correct move temporarily increases the distance).

Scout returned three candidates: (1) Hadrian / Chris Power, 2025-07-17, Factory 3 build-out; (2) Radiant / Doug Bernauer, 2025-12-17, first reactor to mass production; (3) Valar Atomics / Isaiah Taylor, 2025-11-11. Chose (1): it is the only one where the speaker states the unmet precondition out loud AND says money cannot satisfy it ('you could give me a billion dollars and say, go hire 2,000 welders'), which is the exact moment a precondition is promoted to a sub-goal. The two nuclear candidates have richer precondition chains but their states are less numerically paired, and both sit in a crowded nuclear-capacity theme.

Graph decisions: three of the five difference nodes are facts, not derived as the registry's typical_provenance suggests, because Power actually states them ('And so obviously need more capacity', 'coming to us for the schedule and the capacity and stability versus cost', 'we can no longer have that scaled workforce in the country'). Marking them derived would have been dishonest. The two derived differences are the ones nobody states: df2 (4x of floor against 20x of demand, the quotient neither speaker takes) and df5 (the thirty-year software lag read as the gap blocking the 10x-productivity operator). All preconditions and all sub-goals are derived, which is the framework's real contribution here. idea_bearing_slot is precondition; ideas sit on pc2 (0.90) and pc3 (0.70), plus one on sg3 (0.70) in the subgoal slot, which the validator permits. Two fact nodes (op3, the $260M round, and cs5, the software lag) have no fact edge, so they stand alone in the facts-only view; that is true to the source, where the round is announced without a stated link to what it buys and the software lag is offered as a recruiting pitch in a different passage. validate.mjs: 0 errors, 0 warnings on the first run.

tbpn_example.episode_title: Ellison's counter-offer, Chinese H200s, data centers in space (Aaron Ginn, Matt Kalish, Emil Michael, Blake Scholl, Naveen Rao, Ofir Ehrlich, Gorkem Yurtseven)

frameworks.notes:
Research: Inversion (Jacobi's 'invert, always invert'; Munger's 'all I want to know is where I'm going to die, so I'll never go there') plus Gary Klein's pre-mortem, HBR September 2007. Klein's five steps: know the plan; assert the fiasco ('it is a year later and the project has failed'); each member independently writes every reason; consolidate; revisit the plan and engineer safeguards. Mechanism is prospective hindsight (Mitchell, Russo and Pennington 1989: imagining an outcome as already realised raises the ability to name correct reasons by about 30%). It differs from a risk register because failure is asserted as fact, which licenses concrete narrative and lets dissenters speak without disloyalty.

Provenance consequence, decided here: the source gives the plan and the visible risks (goal and most causes are facts); the inversion, the pathways and every safeguard are LLM reasoning. Idea-bearing slot is safeguard: a missing safeguard is often a product someone could sell. Three of the four TBPN safeguards carry an idea (s_parts, s_bond, s_permit).

- Classic fact edges kf5 and kf6 had enclosing spans rather than connectives; both extended to start at 'The director notes three things for the record:' so the clause that attaches the condition to the plan is inside the quote. Still verbatim.
- c_permits: node text said 'the biggest problem with building anything physical'; the speaker says 'a huge problem' and 'much bigger than energy production'. Text corrected and source_ref widened to L4576-L4606, which is where 'such huge delays and huge costs' actually sits.

tbpn_example.episode_title: SpaceX launch deep dive reactions (Josh Reeves, Keller Cliffton, Will Brown, Julia Steinberg, Olivia Moore, Flo Crivello)

frameworks.notes: Research: Cynefin (Dave Snowden, IBM Institute of Knowledge Management, 1999; popularised in Snowden & Boone, 'A Leader's Framework for Decision Making', HBR Nov 2007). Five domains, each with its own causality and its own decision protocol: Clear/Obvious (cause-effect self-evident, best practice, Sense-Categorise-Respond), Complicated (cause-effect knowable with analysis or expertise, good practice, Sense-Analyse-Respond), Complex (cause-effect only coherent in retrospect, emergent practice, Probe-Sense-Respond), Chaotic (no usable cause-effect, novel practice, Act-Sense-Respond), Disorder (you do not know which domain you are in, so everyone argues from their preferred domain). Design decisions: the five domains are structural scaffolding (provenance schema, reserved grey); situations and signals are facts from the source; the classification is a derived edge carrying confidence; the prescribed response is a derived node and is the idea-bearing slot; the page's point is a situation handled with the wrong domain's protocol (a blueprint over an emergent space). Layout: plane, four quadrant regions with Disorder in the centre. Scout returned three candidates (2025-08-27 SpaceX/Starship; 2025-04-04 AI 2027 forecast; 2025-12-04 brand crisis with Katie Deighton). Chose candidate 1 but narrowed it to one continuous stretch (L60-L560) about SpaceX cost decisions, so the example is one coherent moment rather than a tour of the episode; the Cracker Barrel and Lindy material from the same episode was dropped for that reason. Validate: 0 errors, 0 warnings. Added one relation beyond the registry, observed_in (signal belongs to a situation), because the registry relation indicates carries the domain judgment and is therefore always derived; observed_in is what can be a fact edge when one span of the source states an observation as part of a situation, and it is what keeps the facts-only view connected. Known honest limit: in plane mode a situation's quadrant position encodes its classification, which is itself derived, so the facts-only view still shows situations sitting in domains; the classification edges disappear but the placement does not. Noted rather than fixed, because the brief requires the page to read as the Cynefin diagram at a glance. frameworks.name: Wardley Mapping

tbpn_example.episode_title: Google's AI Breakthrough in Cancer, Protein Powders Exposed (Marc Benioff, Eiso Kant, Dante Vaisbort, Alice Bentinck, Eric Seufert, Pim de Witte)

frameworks.notes:
Research (recall): Simon Wardley, from about 2005 at Fotango, answering 'where do we attack?'. A map, not a diagram: it needs an anchor (the user), position relative to that anchor (the value chain, y = visibility to the user, running down from the need to the invisible plumbing) and consistency of movement (x = evolution, left to right through Genesis (I), Custom-built (II), Product +rental (III), Commodity +utility (IV)). Evolution is measured by ubiquity against certainty, not by time, adoption or preference. Climatic patterns used here: everything evolves under supply and demand competition; characteristics change as it evolves (uncharted, uncertain, differentiating at the left; industrialised, metered, undifferentiating at the right); componentisation of a lower layer enables higher-order value; past success breeds inertia. Doctrine: focus on user needs, use a common language, use appropriate methods per stage. Gameplay drawn on: commoditise your complement, buy versus build, ILC. Common misuse: placing components on x by time, by adoption or by how much you like them rather than by the characteristics of the stage; reading y as importance rather than visibility; drawing a value chain with no anchor user, which yields a diagram you cannot move things on.

Scout: three candidates returned (Eiso Kant / Poolside 2025-10-16; Pedro Franceschi / Brex 2025-12-09; hosts on OpenAI's supply chain 2025-10-21). Chose Poolside: a single uninterrupted interview, L4128-L4494, in which one speaker names the anchor user, the need, nine components from coding agents down to grid power, and gives an industrialisation verdict on most of them, including the one that matters most for this library, a layer with demand at 250MW and no vendor to call. The host-analysis episode (2025-10-21) is denser in Wardley vocabulary ('commoditize your compliments') but it is commentary about someone else's stack, so the value chain is asserted rather than owned.

Graph decisions. (a) Components named in the source are facts; where each one sits on the evolution axis is a derived judgement and is recorded as an explicit at_stage edge with a confidence and a rationale, never silently baked into the x position. The x position is a rendering of that edge: hide derived and every at_stage edge disappears, leaving the value chain and four empty stage markers. Nine at_stage edges in the TBPN example, seven in the classic. (b) The four evolution stages are structural scaffolding: slot stage, structural true, provenance schema, no quote, no confidence, excluded from the counts. (c) movement and play are derived, and play is the idea-bearing slot; pl2 and pl3 carry idea sentences. (d) One play is a fact: Kant states his own play on air ('we had to own that vertical stack entirely'), which is unusual and worth showing as a fact node in a slot whose typical provenance is derived. pl1 has only one incoming edge, the derived enables from m1, so it floats in the facts-only view; a depends_on edge from a play down to a component was drafted and removed because depends_on is defined as component-to-component and using it for a play would blur the relation. (e) Frontier intelligence (c4) is placed at Product, not Commodity, at confidence 0.7: Kant calls intelligence a commodity but says in the same breath that only a small number of companies can create it, which is a handful of substitutable suppliers, i.e. stage III. His 'commodity' is read as the destination, which is what movement m1 records. The delivery form, tokens behind an API (c3), is placed at Commodity at 0.85 because he says outright that it is his commodity business. (f) Fact edges follow SPEC 3 strictly: two fact endpoints plus a quoted connective. Seven of the twelve TBPN value-chain edges qualify; the rest (user-to-need joins, the coding-agent fulfilment, shell-to-energy) are derived, because the speaker names both ends in different breaths. Edge te2 (coding agents depend on intelligence) is a fact edge whose connective is spoken by the host, not by Kant: both endpoints are fact nodes and one speaker's turn states the connection, which is the criterion in SPEC 3, so it is marked fact and flagged here. (g) Classic example: an original scenario in the shape of Wardley's canonical 'cup of tea' teaching map, written as a shop owner's notes so that every fact node has a verbatim span to quote. Its Genesis band is empty on purpose, which is the point of the second play. (h) Layout: plane, x = evolution -60..60 with the four bands as regions labelled by stage characteristics rather than stage names (the stage names live on the schema nodes and the axis ticks carry I-IV), y = value chain 34 down to -68 with the anchor user at the top; a dashed guide at y=-56 separates the map from the row of plays read off it.

Validate after the scaffold: 0 errors, 0 warnings.

(c) c3 (Tokens behind an API) carries no entities because its text names no company: Kant states the point generically ('you're in two businesses'). The builder kept plane mode for both examples, widened the evolution axis to +/-64 so the four bands use the available width, gave every depends_on / needs / fulfilled_by edge a downward run (te4 and, found by the builder, ce8 were horizontal), pulled the right-edge nodes in, re-spaced the stage row, region captions and guide label, and shortened five labels (s1-s4 in both examples, with the Roman numerals moved to the x-axis ticks, and pl3 to 'Productise deployment'). frameworks.name: OODA Loop

tbpn_example.episode_title: Code Red, AWS CEO Joins, Tae Kim Tells All (Matt Garman, Tae Kim, Tarek Mansour, Matt Mullenweg, Jason Fried)

frameworks.notes: Research step: John Boyd's OODA loop, developed from Aerial Attack Study (1964) and Energy-Maneuverability theory, formalised in the briefings Patterns of Conflict and The Essence of Winning and Losing (1996). Four phases Observe, Orient, Decide, Act, but the real content is that Orientation is the big outer loop: it is shaped by genetic heritage, cultural tradition, previous experience and new information, and it both filters observation and feeds implicit guidance and control directly to action, bypassing explicit Decide. Boyd's operational claim is not 'be fast' but 'operate inside the adversary's OODA loop' - generate a rapidly changing environment the adversary cannot orient to, so his decisions are answers to a world that has already moved. Common misuse: reading OODA as a tidy four-box sequential cycle (a PDCA lookalike), dropping the orientation feedback arrows and the adversary entirely. Design decision for this framework: model TWO competing actors' loops so that one actor's action node feeds the other actor's observation node, and cycle-time asymmetry is visible. | Scout returned three candidates: (1) Google vs OpenAI Gemini 3 code red 2025-12-02, (2) Meta vs OpenAI comp raid 2025-06-30, (3) Paramount vs Netflix counter-bid 2025-12-09. Chose (1): it is the only candidate where both actors' loops are shown closing on each other across two turns (ChatGPT 2022 -> Google's code red -> a decade of TPUs -> Gemini 3 -> OpenAI's code red), and the cycle-time asymmetry is stated in units on the record (a decade of silicon vs an answer due now). (3) would have duplicated the episode already used by inversion-premortem. | Validator: 0 errors, 0 warnings. Shortened two classic labels (c_s_or2, c_m_lose) to stay inside 40 chars before the scaffold commit. | Design decisions: two interlocking rings, one per actor, actor node at each ring centre with performed_by spokes; idea_bearing_slot is `orientation`, because for OODA the exploitable thing is the blind spot in a rival's filter, and three derived orientation nodes carry `idea` (g_orient, o_or_bench, o_or_subs). | SPEC 3 split rule is demonstrated on OpenAI's orientation: o_or_stated is a FACT node in the orientation slot (Mark Chen's own after-the-fact admission about reasoning vs pre-training), and o_or_bench / o_or_subs are the derived halves the speakers never state. | te20 (o_dec_personalize -> o_act_chen, 0.55) is deliberately below 0.65: the action slot on OpenAI's side has only a public promise inside the two-week window, and the rationale says so. | Resume 2026-09-10: the first viz builder was killed by a usage limit before reporting. frameworks.notes: Research: PDCA originates with Shewhart's three-step specification-production-inspection cycle (1939), turned by Deming into a four-step learning loop and taught in Japan from 1950; Deming later renamed Check to Study (PDSA) precisely because 'check' invites inspection rather than comparison against a prediction. The four phases are scaffolding (structural slot `phase`, provenance schema, reserved grey). The framework's sharp edge: the Plan phase's `hypothesis` - what was expected to happen and why - is almost never stated, so it must be derived; a pilot whose hypothesis cannot be recovered was not an experiment. Classic misuse: PDCA as a project-status ritual where Check reports that the work was done rather than what it was measured against. | Scout returned three candidates: (1) Ramp Labs / Ramp Sheets, 2025-11-24; (2) CodeRabbit on GPT-5 golden dataset, 2025-08-07; (3) Super.com's abandoned goods business, 2025-08-28. Chose (1): it is the only one that narrates two full turns of the same cycle, it has a quoted pivot decision AND a quoted hard number (99% of Looms showed a spreadsheet), and its second turn has the thin Check the framework is built to expose. (2) was rejected because the extraction mis-attributes its speaker and its Act is a pricing non-decision; (3) has no number attached to the experiment it measures. | Design decisions: the four phases are schema nodes in the structural `phase` slot (grey, reserved), and every content node carries an in_phase edge to its phase, the way Ishikawa hangs causes on ribs; a relation `advances_to` was added (registry ids all kept) so the four phase markers form a visible cycle that survives the facts-only view. | Provenance calls: the `hypothesis` slot is derived in both TBPN turns (h1, h2) - the source states that an experiment was run and never what it predicted, which is the framework's sharpest contribution. Both TBPN `metric` nodes for the loops that declared nothing (m1, m3) are derived; f_look is a fact metric because the team states the measurement it deliberately took. `yields` is used pilot->measurement as a fact edge wherever a speaker jumps straight from the trial to a number with no metric in between (te_y1f, te_y3f), which makes the thin Check structurally visible: hide the derived layer and the Check phase has numbers with nothing to read them against. The baseline measurement c_base / f_reject sit in the Plan and Check phases respectively per Deming's own ordering (study the current process in Plan). | validate: 0 errors, 0 warnings on the first run. | README: previous parent was interrupted after the README child wrote the file; the resuming parent verified it programmatically against graph.json (every non-schema node id, text, quote, confidence, rationale and idea present verbatim; source text verbatim; all six relative links resolve) and kept it. frameworks.name: Systems Thinking

frameworks.notes:
Research: Forrester's Industrial Dynamics (1961), Meadows' Thinking in Systems (2008) and her 1999 Leverage Points essay, Senge's Fifth Discipline (1990), Sterman's Business Dynamics (2000). Registry slot ids kept unchanged.

Provenance design decisions. (1) Stocks, flows and variables are mostly facts in both examples: speakers describe accumulations and rates constantly without ever calling them stocks or flows, so the extraction work is recognition, not inference. (2) Every loop node is derived, in both examples, and that is the rule rather than an accident: a closed chain of influence is never stated. In the TBPN example the individual arrows of R1, R2 and B1 are largely quotable (10 of 44 edges are fact edges and they are concentrated on the loops' own links), which makes the point sharply: the data gives you the arrows, the framework gives you the circle and its sign. (3) Edge polarity is carried in the edge `label` field as + or -, per SPEC 4, so a reader can do the sign arithmetic that decides reinforcing vs balancing. (4) Delays are split rather than forced into one provenance: d_lead / cd_order / cd_ship are facts because the speakers state the lags verbatim, while d_overshoot / cd_overshoot are derived, because the claim that a lag inside a balancing loop converts correction into oscillation is the framework's general result and is what explains the observed overshoot. (5) leverage_point is the idea-bearing slot, and lp_delay deliberately carries no `idea` field: it is the low-rank Meadows intervention (9th, delays) that the whole market is already pulling, included as the control case so the hierarchy does visible work against lp_rule (rules, 6th) and lp_info (information flows, 6th), which do carry ideas.

Classic example is the MIT Beer Distribution Game, with a scenario text written for this page so the fact nodes have something verbatim to quote. It was chosen because it is the canonical demonstration that a delay inside a balancing loop produces oscillation, and because its textbook leverage point is literally an information flow, which is Meadows' own argument. R1 there (the shortage spiral) has all four of its arrows quoted from the scenario text and two negative links, so the reinforcing sign is arithmetic rather than taste.
